title: When things go wrong
goal: Cope in Indonesian when something goes wrong: report a theft to the police, get the *surat keterangan kehilangan*, talk to a doctor in A&E, deal with insurance, and complain in writing without losing your manners.
bekal: make a police report: *Saya mau melaporkan kehilangan dompet*
describe an injury and understand the doctor: *terpeleset, bengkak, rawat jalan*
ask for the documents an insurance claim needs: *surat keterangan medis, kuitansi asli*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di kantor polisi
dialogs.intro: A Tuesday in September, in Magelang. Sarah went to Pasar Rejowinangun to buy salak for the homestay, and came back without her wallet. Now she is at the service desk (SPKT) of the town's police station.

notes: **Ada yang bisa kami bantu?** The standard opening of any service desk, from banks to police stations: “is there something we can help with?”. Note *kami*, not *saya*: the officer speaks for the institution. The desk itself is the *SPKT* (*Sentra Pelayanan Kepolisian Terpadu*), the integrated service centre found in every police station.

**Melaporkan kehilangan.** *Kehilangan* is both the verb “to lose” (*Saya kehilangan dompet*) and the noun “loss”. The paper Sarah receives is officially the *Surat Keterangan Tanda Lapor Kehilangan* (SKTLK), but everyone calls it *surat kehilangan*. Banks, Immigration and phone shops all ask for it.
**Justru KITAS saya…** *Justru* here means “that's exactly the problem”: it turns the officer's request back on itself. Very natural, and more polite than *Tidak bisa, Pak*.

**Kecopetan** is the adversative *ke-…-an* from A2: something bad happened **to** you. *Copet* is a pickpocket, *dicopet* is to be pickpocketed. Its cousins: *kecurian* (robbed, burgled), *kemalingan* (burgled, from *maling*, thief), *kebobolan* (broken into).

**Mohon disebutkan, mohon dicek.** Officials make requests with *mohon* + a passive verb, exactly like the notices in A2 Unit 15. It is courteous and impersonal at once. You answer it simply, with no need to repeat the verb.

**Layanan ini gratis.** Making a police report costs nothing, and police stations display signs saying *Tidak dipungut biaya* (no fee is charged). *Hati-hati di jalan* (“careful on the road”) is the standard goodbye to someone who is leaving, from a friend or a police officer alike.

grammars.title: Lapor and hilang: two word families for the counter
body: You will hear every member of these two families in any office where something is reported, from a police station to a hotel reception.

head: Word
English
Example
rows: to make a report, to report in

after: *Kehilangan* just states the loss; *menghilangkan* blames somebody for it. *Maaf, saya menghilangkan buku Ibu* is an honest confession: “I've lost your book.” Ads use the second meaning too: *menghilangkan noda* (removes stains).
The *terlapor* is the person who has been reported, the accused. You will meet it in news stories rather than at the desk.

grammars.title: Answering an official's questions
body: Officials ask in a compact, slightly formal style. Recognise the question and answer with the information only; you do not need to match their register.

head: The official says
What they want
You answer
rows: your name (on a form, a booking)

after: *Kronologi* (chronology) is the word for “what happened, step by step”, and you will be asked for it after any accident, theft or dispute. Tell it with the sequencers from A2 Unit 20: *awalnya, lalu, setelah itu, akhirnya*.

dialogs.intro: Ten days later. A Dutch guest at one of the homestays, Mevrouw Anke, slipped in the bathroom and hit her head. Sarah has brought her to the A&E (IGD) of the district hospital in Muntilan and talks to the doctor on duty.

notes: **Mbak keluarga pasien?** Hospitals want to know who is responsible for a patient, and in Indonesia that is normally the family, who also stay, feed and look after them. A friend or colleague who brings someone in is called the *penanggung jawab* (the person responsible) for the paperwork.

**Dok** is the short address for a doctor, just as *Pak* and *Bu* are. In writing, a medical doctor is *dr.* in lower case (*dr. Fitri*); *Dr.* with a capital is a PhD, like Dr. Lestari. Indonesians find the difference obvious and foreigners never notice it.

**Terpeleset** is *ter-* of accident: to slip without meaning to. Its neighbours: *terjatuh* (to fall over), *tersandung* (to trip), *terkilir* (to sprain), *tergores* (to get scratched). Compare A2 Unit 11.

**Rontgen** (from the name of the German physicist) is the everyday word for an X-ray, and it becomes a verb with no prefix at all: *Kita rontgen dulu*, *sudah dirontgen*. Hospitals may also write *foto sinar-X*.

**Rawat inap, rawat jalan.** *Rawat* means to look after. *Rawat inap* (care with an overnight stay) is inpatient treatment; *rawat jalan* (care while walking) is outpatient treatment. ⚠️ *Kontrol* is a false friend: it means a follow-up check-up, not “control”.
**Syukurlah** (thank God, thank goodness) is *syukur* (gratitude) + the *-lah* of Unit 17. Muslims may say *Alhamdulillah* in the same place; *syukurlah* works for everyone.

grammars.title: Describing an injury
body: Most injury words are either *ter-* verbs (it happened to you by accident) or plain adjectives describing the result. Put them together and you have the whole story.

head: What happened
The result
English
rows: knocked against something; a cut, wounded
hit by a motorbike; a broken bone

after: Say where it hurts with *sakit* or the body part + *-nya*: *Kepalanya terbentur pintu* (she hit her head on the door), *Kaki saya sakit* (my foot hurts). *Pusing* is dizzy or a headache, *mual* is nauseous.
⚠️ *Patah* is for things that snap: bones, sticks, pencils. A broken phone or car is *rusak*; a broken glass is *pecah*.

blocks.text: Indonesian hospitals are organised in *instalasi* and *bagian* (departments). You go in through the IGD in an emergency and through the *poli* (outpatient clinic) otherwise.

blocks.title: Emergency numbers
items: *112* — national emergency number, works from any phone
*113* — fire brigade (*pemadam kebakaran*, usually shortened to *damkar*)
*118* or *119* — ambulance (*ambulans*), depending on the region

blocks.text: Indonesians complain softly and in writing if they can. A complaint that opens with courtesy and ends with a request gets answered; one that opens with anger gets filed. The spoken word is *komplain*; the standard one is *keluhan* or *pengaduan*.

head: Step
Indonesian
English
rows: *Dengan hormat, saya ingin menyampaikan keluhan mengenai…*
I would like to raise a complaint about…
I ask that this be followed up promptly.
*Atas perhatian dan kerja samanya, saya ucapkan terima kasih.*
Thank you for your attention and cooperation.

blocks.text: In speech the shape is the same, only shorter: *Maaf, Mas, saya mau komplain sedikit. Kamarnya belum dibersihkan dari kemarin. Bisa dibantu?* The *Bisa dibantu?* at the end is what makes it work.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
